 Here's the Average Social Security Benefit of 88-Year-Old Americans (How Do You Compare?)
 Chris Lewis, CEPF 2026년 11월 7일 토 오전 10:03 UTC 0 
 By the time you're 88, Social Security is a big part of your monthly income. Considering the various factors that determined your
 benefit amount in the first place, it's natural to wonder how you compare to
 your peers.
 This is important to understand if you're living on just
 Social Security, as your monthly check is expected to cover every bill.
 Here's the average Social Security benefit at 88 and why your own number may
 differ.
 Find Out: 13 moves seniors could benefit from but often forget about. 
 What is the average Social Security benefit of an 88-year-old?
 The average 88-year-old collecting Social Security benefits received $1,983.29 a
 month at the end of December 2025, according to Social Security Administration
 (SSA) data. That's about $23,800 a year.
 SSA's count included 598,324 retired workers aged 88. Their averages differ by
 sex:
 Men: $2,131.29 a month
 Women: $1,859.56 a month
 Overall: $1,983.29 a month
 Men received $271.73 more per month on average, or about $3,261 more per year.
 Across all ages, the average retired worker received $2,071.30, about $88 more
 than the average 88-year-old.
 These figures cover only retired-worker beneficiaries, who worked long enough to
 qualify on their own records. Someone who collects only as a spouse or survivor
 isn't included, and those benefits follow different rules.

 Why men collect more Social Security than women at 88
 The SSA bases your retirement benefit on your highest 35 years of earnings , so
 differences in pay and years worked show up in retirement checks.
 Women, on average, earn less and work fewer hours and years than men, according
 to a review in SSA's Social Security Bulletin. One reason is that women are more
 likely to pause their careers to care for family.
 That earnings gap was considerably wider during the working years of today's
 88-year-olds. In 1990, when they were in their early 50s, women ages 50 to 59
 had median annual earnings equal to just 50.1% of men's, compared with 67.5% in
 2019, according to SSA data.
 Spousal and survivor benefits help narrow that gap, particularly for women, who
 are far more likely than men to qualify for benefits based on a spouse's
 earnings record, according to SSA data. 
 The SSA's table separates out retirees who
 also qualify for a higher benefit on another person's record, such as a widow's
 benefit. At 88, that group included 175,014 women but only 7,281 men. Women relying on their own record alone averaged $1,678.00 a
 month, compared with $2,137.70 for men, a gap of $459.70.
 How your work record changes your benefit amount
 The same 35-year formula explains much of the spread between any two retirees. The SSA counts a zero for each year without earnings, so someone with 25 years of
 work has 10 zeros averaged in. Low-earning years also lower the average, even in
 a full 35-year career, while higher earnings raise it.

 Why the age you claimed still affects your check at 88
 The SSA reduces benefits for each month you collect before full retirement age. If
 you wait past full retirement age, you earn delayed retirement credits for each
 month you hold off, up to age 70.
 For people born in 1937 and 1938, those credits added 6.5% for each year of
 waiting. Two 88-year-olds with identical work records may collect very different
 amounts if one started at 62 and the other waited until 70. SSA's table doesn't
 show when each retiree claimed, so the 88-year-old average mixes early and late
 claimers.
 How decades of cost-of-living raises changed the payment
 Since 1975, automatic cost-of-living adjustments (COLAs) have raised benefits in
 line with inflation. An 88-year-old who claimed at 62 in 1999 has received every
 adjustment since January 2000, from no increase in 2010, 2011, and 2016 to 8.7%
 in 2023.
 COLAs are percentages, so a smaller
 benefit gets a smaller dollar raise, and they don't undo a reduction for
 claiming early.
 How your benefit fits with your other retirement income
 If you collect $1,600 a month, you're about $383 below the 88-year-old average,
 or roughly $4,600 a year. Still, that information doesn't tell you whether
 you're financially secure.
 A retiree with a paid-off home and a pension may be better off on a smaller
 check than someone with a larger benefit and high rent or medical bills. Add up
 your Social Security, any pension, and the amounts you withdraw from savings or
 retirement accounts, then compare that monthly total to your costs.
 If you're comparing your bank deposit with the average, keep in mind that SSA
 usually deducts Medicare premiums from monthly benefits. Your deposit may be
 smaller than your full benefit.

 How to check your own Social Security benefit
 For your own numbers, use your my Social Security account. If you receive
 benefits, the account lets you print a benefit verification letter and see your
 annual cost-of-living adjustment amount.
 The averages in this article are general information rather than personalized
 advice. If your payment looks wrong or you're not sure which benefit you
 receive, contact SSA directly.
 Bottom line
 Coming in under the average doesn't mean you're behind. What counts at 88 is
 whether your Social Security and other income cover your bills, and that depends
 on your own record and costs.
 If your income and savings are limited, look into Medicare's Extra Help
 program. It lowers or cuts Medicare Part D costs, such as deductibles and
 copays, and SSA accepts applications at any time, online or by calling
 1-800-772-1213. Eligibility depends on your income and resources, so gather bank
 statements and retirement account balances before you apply. It's a practical
 way to maximize
 your senior benefits .
 FAQs
 Can an 88-year-old receive a deceased spouse's Social Security benefit?
 You may qualify for survivor benefits if your spouse has died. If you already receive retirement benefits, Social Security generally pays the higher amount you qualify for rather than adding two full benefits together. Contact SSA to check whether a survivor benefit could increase your payment.
 Do retirement account withdrawals reduce Social Security benefits at 88?
 Withdrawals from an IRA or other retirement account do not directly reduce your Social Security retirement benefit. Social Security does not count those withdrawals as earnings for its earnings test, and that test no longer applies once you reach full retirement age.
 What help is available if Medicare costs take too much of your Social Security check?
 A Medicare Savings Program may help pay your Part B premium and, depending on the program, other Medicare expenses. You apply through your state, and eligibility rules vary. Some states allow higher income or resource levels than the federal guidelines, so checking your eligibility can be worthwhile.
